section.title: Give Thanks, for He Is Good
section.sectionRationale: The opening psalm of Book V, Psalms 107 to 150, which answers the exile and gathers the redeemed community into a fresh season of praise. Its opening line, Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good, His loving devotion endures forever, deliberately picks up the refrain that closed Psalm 106 and Book IV, and its call for the redeemed of the LORD to say so, verse 2, invites the whole congregation, gathered from every direction, to tell their own stories of rescue.
section.thesis: The LORD redeems His people out of four representative distresses, wandering, imprisonment, sickness, and the storm at sea, always in answer to a desperate cry, so that every rescued soul, whatever the shape of the trouble, owes Him the same public thanksgiving and the same wise consideration of His steadfast love.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: give thanks, let the redeemed say so, verses 1 to 3; wanderers gathered and fed, verses 4 to 9; prisoners set free, verses 10 to 16; fools healed from the brink of death, verses 17 to 22; sailors delivered from the storm, verses 23 to 32; the LORD who reverses fortunes, verses 33 to 38; and a closing judgment, mercy, and call to wisdom, verses 39 to 43.

units.label: Let the redeemed of the LORD say so
units.note: give thanks, let the redeemed say so

verses.text: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.
Let the {{gaal|redeemed}} of the LORD say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the enemy
and gathered from the lands, from east and west, from north and south.

units.label: He led them on a straight path

verses.text: Some wandered in desert wastelands, finding no path to a city in which to dwell.
They were hungry and thirsty; their soul fainted within them.
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He delivered them from their distress.
He led them on a straight path to reach a city where they could live.
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.
For He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things.
Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and chains,
because they rebelled against the words of God and despised the counsel of the Most High.
He humbled their hearts with hard labor; they stumbled, and there was no one to help.
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress.
He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death and broke away their chains.
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.
For He has broken down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron.

units.label: He sent forth His word and healed them
units.note: fools healed from the brink of death

verses.text: Fools, in their rebellious ways, and through their iniquities, suffered affliction.
They loathed all food and drew near to the gates of death.
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He saved them from their distress.
He sent forth His word and healed them; He rescued them from the Pit.
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.
Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing.

units.label: He calmed the storm to a whisper

verses.text: Others went out to sea in ships, conducting trade on the mighty waters.
They saw the works of the LORD, and His wonders in the deep.
For He spoke and raised a tempest that lifted the waves of the sea.
They mounted up to the heavens, then sunk to the depths; their courage melted in their anguish.
They reeled and staggered like drunkards, and all their skill was useless.
Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble, and He brought them out of their distress.
He {{damam|calmed}} the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed.
They rejoiced in the silence, and He guided them to the harbor they desired.
Let them give thanks to the LORD for His loving devotion and His wonders to the sons of men.
Let them exalt Him in the assembly of the people and praise Him in the council of the elders.

units.label: He turns a desert into pools of water

verses.text: He turns rivers into deserts, springs of water into thirsty ground,
and fruitful land into fields of salt, because of the wickedness of its dwellers.
He turns a desert into pools of water and a dry land into flowing springs.
He causes the hungry to settle there, that they may establish a city in which to dwell.
They sow fields and plant vineyards that yield a fruitful harvest.
He blesses them, and they multiply greatly; He does not let their herds diminish.

units.label: Let him who is wise pay heed
units.note: judgment, mercy, and a closing call to wisdom

verses.text: When they are decreased and humbled by oppression, evil, and sorrow,
He pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.
But He lifts the needy from affliction and increases their families like flocks.
The upright see and rejoice, and all iniquity shuts its mouth.
Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD.

gaal.gloss: To redeem, to act as a kinsman-redeemer who buys back or rescues at cost. The psalm's opening call, let the redeemed say so, verse 2, invites every rescued person to publicly testify to this costly deliverance.

damam.gloss: To be silent, still, hushed. God calms the raging storm to this stillness, verse 29, the same divine authority Jesus exercises when He rebukes the wind and sea and says, Peace, be still, Mark 4:39.

basic.context: Opening Book V of the Psalter, this psalm gathers the voices of the redeemed, likely returning exiles among them, verse 3, and invites them to tell their own rescue stories under four pictures: wanderers lost and fed, prisoners freed, the sick healed, and sailors saved from the storm. Each scene follows the same pattern, crisis, cry, and rescue, ending in a call to give thanks.
basic.hermeneutics: The four scenes function as representative categories into which any sufferer's story can be read, not merely as four unrelated historical anecdotes; the repeated refrain, let them give thanks, makes this an invitation for the reader's own testimony, not just a report of what God once did for others.
basic.originalLanguages: Those saved are the geulim, the gaal, redeemed, verse 2, those bought back at cost from the enemy's hand. The storm's fury is calmed to damam, stillness, verse 29, the very word and divine authority Jesus later claims for Himself over the sea.
basic.typology: The sailors' cry answered by a calmed sea, verses 23-30, directly anticipates Jesus calming the storm on the Sea of Galilee, Mark 4:35-41, where the disciples ask the very question this psalm answers: who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him.
basic.christ: Jesus' calming of the storm, Mark 4:35-41, deliberately echoes this psalm's fourth scene, He commands the wind and waves with the same word, be still, damam, that this psalm attributes to the LORD alone, verse 29, revealing His own divine identity to disciples who had sung this psalm all their lives.
basic.god: God is shown hearing every kind of cry, from wanderers lost in the wilderness to prisoners in chains to the sick at death's door to sailors terrified at sea, and answering each with the same undeserved rescue, all traced back to His enduring loving devotion, the psalm's opening and closing note.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 4:35-41 shows Jesus calming the storm with the same authority this psalm ascribes to God. Luke 4:18 shows Jesus proclaiming liberty to captives, echoing the psalm's prisoners set free. Isaiah 43:5-7 promises the gathering from every direction that this psalm celebrates as already underway.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's fourfold testimony of rescue, wanderers fed, prisoners freed, the sick healed, sailors saved, is the pattern that every believer's own redemption follows, and it climaxes in Christ, who redeems from the ultimate distress of sin and death and who commands the very storms this psalm describes.

context.literary:
The psalm has a rare double shape: a refrain-driven centre set inside a frame. The frame is verses 1 to 3 at the start and verses 33 to 43 at the end, a call to the redeemed and a meditation on how the LORD reverses fortunes. Between them four scenes run on a nearly mechanical template, trouble, cry, rescue, thanks, but each scene alters the template just enough to keep it alive. The first scene does not say why the sufferers were in trouble, and the fourth gives no human cause; the second and third say it was their own rebellion, verses 11 and 17; and the fourth says the LORD Himself raised the storm, verse 25. So the four pictures ask the hearer to consider every possible cause of distress, bad luck, human sin, divine discipline, and to see that the same response is open in each case.

The refrain in verses 6, 13, 19 and 28 is identical word for word, 'Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble,' and the second refrain of thanks in verses 8, 15, 21 and 31 is identical too. The repetition is so tight that the small variations stand out. In the third scene the thanks refrain is followed by a command to bring thank offerings, verse 22, and in the fourth by a command to praise in the assembly, verse 32. The thanksgiving moves from the private to the public, from the heart to the temple court.

The fourth scene is also the longest by far, ten verses against six or seven for the others, and it is the only one with a vivid sequence of images: tempest, mountain-high waves, a staggering crew, a sudden hush and a safe harbour. It is the climactic scene of the series, and its quiet ending, 'They rejoiced in the silence,' verse 30, is the emotional peak.

The closing section, verses 33 to 43, shifts from narrative to something like wisdom poetry. Rivers become desert and desert becomes springs, the proud are humbled and the needy are lifted, and the last verse addresses the reader directly: 'Let him who is wise pay heed.' The psalm ends by turning stories into a lesson.
context.historical:
The psalm opens Book V and speaks of people gathered 'from the lands, from east and west, from north and south,' verse 3. The footnote notes that the Hebrew has 'north and the sea', which in Israelite geography means the Mediterranean to the west or, in some readings, the south. The language fits the return from Babylon in the sixth century and after, when exiles came home from several directions, Isaiah 43:5 and 6. But the psalm does not name the exile, and it deliberately speaks in categories open to every person who has been rescued.

The four settings were all common in the world of ancient Israel. Desert caravans that lost their way and ran out of water were an everyday danger. Debt slavery and prison were realities, and so was serious illness. The picture of merchants who 'went out to sea in ships, conducting trade on the mighty waters' is the more surprising, because Israel was not a seafaring nation. The sea was a symbol of chaos in Israelite thought, Psalm 93:3 and 4, and sailors who survived a storm were held in awe as people who had seen the works of the LORD 'in the deep,' verse 24.

Later Jewish tradition drew a practice from the psalm. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, teaches that four kinds of people must give thanks: those who have crossed the sea, those who have crossed a desert, those who have recovered from sickness, and those who have been released from prison. The custom of a thanksgiving blessing after surviving danger grew from this reading. It shows how naturally the first hearers took the four scenes as a list of classic situations needing a public testimony.

The 'thanksgiving sacrifices' of verse 22 refer to the todah offering described in Leviticus 7:12, a fellowship sacrifice eaten with others in the days after deliverance. Someone who had been rescued would bring an animal, bread and wine to the sanctuary and tell the story in front of friends. The psalm is shaped to be sung at such an occasion.
context.canonical:
Psalm 107 begins with the same words that close Psalm 106, 'Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever,' and answers its last prayer, 'gather us from the nations,' Psalm 106:47, with the word 'gathered from the lands,' verse 3. The book boundary is therefore a seam and not a break. The people who ended Book IV pleading for rescue begin Book V telling the story of those who have been rescued.

The refrain 'His loving devotion endures forever' recurs at the head of Psalm 118 and Psalm 136, which suggests a stream of liturgy running through Book V. The theme of redemption from the enemy's hand also links to the Exodus, where the LORD redeemed Israel, Exodus 15:13, and to the prophets, who call the returning exiles 'the redeemed of the LORD,' Isaiah 62:12 and 35:9. When Isaiah describes the highway on which 'the redeemed will walk' and 'return and enter Zion with singing,' he sounds like the psalm in prophetic form.

Several of the psalm's images are reused throughout Scripture. The turning of desert into pools, verse 35, repeats Isaiah 41:18, where the LORD says He will turn the desert into a pool of water. The 'gates of bronze' and 'bars of iron' that He breaks, verse 16, echo Isaiah 45:2, where the same words are used of the doors opened for Cyrus. The statement that He 'sent forth His word and healed them,' verse 20, resonates with Isaiah 55:11 and Psalm 147:15, where His word runs swiftly and accomplishes what He sends it to do.

The New Testament takes up the psalm in the Gospels, where Jesus does what verse 20 and verse 29 say the LORD does. He heals with a word, Matthew 8:8 and 16, and He silences a storm, Mark 4:39. The Magnificat's line 'He has filled the hungry with good things,' Luke 1:53, echoes verse 9, and the gathering from every direction becomes the gathering of the nations in Revelation 7:9. The psalm ends by calling the wise to consider the LORD's loving devotion, and Hosea 14:9 closes the prophets with a similar summons.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wants the community to learn a discipline of testimony. He does not ask the redeemed to keep their rescue private. 'Let the redeemed of the LORD say so,' verse 2, is an instruction to speak, and the repeated 'Let them give thanks' is a liturgical cue for a congregation to respond. He is training people to tell their stories in a particular way, naming the trouble honestly, naming the cry, and giving the LORD, and not luck or their own skill, the credit for the outcome. The sailors' 'all their skill was useless,' verse 27, is the clearest example of a story where human competence runs out and God's help begins.

He also intends the hearer to see the wide mercy of God. The four groups have different histories, and the psalm does not claim all were innocent. Some suffered for their rebellion, verses 11 and 17, and God still heard them. The message is that the door of mercy is not closed by the cause of the distress. At the same time, the psalm is no cheap comfort. It speaks of hard labour, gates of death and the pit, and it leaves the reader with the sobering reversals of verses 33 to 40, in which the LORD can turn fruitful land into salt flats.

The closing line is therefore the key to his purpose. 'Let him who is wise pay heed to these things.' The stories are not merely to be admired. They are to be pondered until the hearer can see the pattern of God's loving devotion in his own life.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes four kinds of rescue and does not promise that every wanderer, prisoner, sick person or sailor in trouble will be delivered on earth. It is a record of those who were, and its call is to thanksgiving. Reading it as a guarantee that prayer always ends in rescue would turn a testimony into a formula, and the Bible itself holds the other side, as in Psalm 88 or Habakkuk 3:17 to 19.

The psalm's statements about cause and effect also need care. Verses 11 and 17 say that some trouble came from rebellion and folly. They do not say that all suffering has that cause, and Jesus rejected that inference when His disciples asked whether a man was born blind because of sin, John 9:2 and 3. The psalm gives categories of suffering and does not offer a diagnosis for every case.

What it prescribes clearly is the response: cry out, give thanks and tell others. The words 'in the assembly of the people' and 'in the council of the elders,' verse 32, make clear that gratitude is meant to be public. A believer who has been helped is meant to say so in the gathered community, both to honour God and to give hope to those still in the trouble. And the final call to wisdom, verse 43, asks the reader to build a habit of noticing God's work, not only of reacting to crises.

debates.question: Are the four scenes a record of real groups, or literary categories for every sufferer?

views.label: Real situations, probably tied to the return from exile
views.case: The opening verses speak of those 'redeemed from the hand of the enemy' and 'gathered from the lands,' which suggests returning exiles. Desert wandering, imprisonment, sickness and sea travel are all plausible experiences along that journey, and the Talmud's later list of four thanksgivings treats them as real situations.

views.label: Stylised categories chosen for their range
views.case: The scenes follow identical templates and the details stay general. There are no names, places or dates. A desert, a prison, a sickbed and a ship together cover land, confinement, body and sea, which is nearly a map of human danger. On this view the psalmist built a series of types so that any hearer could place himself in one of them.

debates.bearing: Nothing in the psalm requires choosing between these. A form can be rooted in real events and still be shaped to include everyone. The point for the reader is that the pattern, trouble, cry, rescue, thanks, is open to him too, whether or not he can match his trouble to one of the four.

debates.question: Does the psalm teach that suffering is caused by sin?

views.label: Yes, in the cases it names
views.case: Verse 11 says prisoners were bound because they rebelled against God's words, and verse 17 says fools suffered affliction through their iniquities. Verses 33 to 34 add that fruitful land becomes salt because of its dwellers' wickedness. On this reading the psalm affirms a moral order in which wrongdoing brings trouble.

views.label: Only in some cases, and not as a general rule
views.case: The first and fourth scenes give no cause at all, and the sailors were simply doing their trade when the storm came. The psalm also records that the same cry and the same mercy answer all four scenes, whatever the cause. Jesus' answer in John 9:3 and His comment on the fallen tower in Luke 13:1 to 5 confirm that one cannot read guilt from suffering.

debates.bearing: The psalm holds both: some suffering is the fruit of folly, and some is not, and in both God hears the cry. A wise reader will use the first truth as a warning for himself and will refuse to use it as an accusation against someone else.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm's first key word is gaal, 'redeemed,' in verse 2. The root describes a family duty. A go'el was a near relative who bought back land that had been sold, Leviticus 25:25, or a kinsman who married a childless widow and redeemed her family's name, as Boaz does in Ruth 4. When the prophets speak of God as the Redeemer of Israel, Isaiah 43:1 and 44:22, they draw on this family image: God acts as a kinsman who will not let His own be lost. So 'the redeemed of the LORD' are not strangers freed by a distant power but people whose nearest Relative has come for them. The same title is given to returning Zion in Isaiah 62:12.

The refrain of thanks uses the root yadah, 'give thanks,' which is the verb of public confession as well as gratitude. To thank in Hebrew is to say aloud what someone has done. That is why verse 2 says 'say so' and why the sacrifices of verse 22 are joined to 'declare His works.' The word for the offering, todah, comes from the same root, and the todah was a sacrifice that was also a story told.

In the third scene the sufferers are called 'fools,' from evilim. The word belongs to the vocabulary of Proverbs, where fools 'despise wisdom and instruction,' Proverbs 1:7. It does not mean a lack of intellect but a refusal to listen. That matches verse 11, where the prisoners 'despised the counsel of the Most High.' The verb 'despised' there is the same attitude the foolish take to wisdom. The healing that follows comes by a word, verse 20, and in Hebrew thought a word is not a weak thing but an act that accomplishes what it says, as in Genesis 1.

The fourth scene contains a delicate Hebrew phrase in verse 29. The LORD makes the storm stand 'to a whisper,' using the noun demamah, which is the word for the 'still, small voice' in which God spoke to Elijah, 1 Kings 19:12. The same word thus describes the sound of God's presence at Horeb and the sound of the sea at rest. The footnote also notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls read 'the waves of the sea' where the traditional Hebrew text has 'their waves,' a small difference that does not change the sense.

Verse 27 describes the sailors' helplessness, and the footnote gives two literal alternatives: 'all their wisdom was swallowed up' or 'they were at their wits' end.' The Hebrew idiom is of skill that is consumed by the sea, which makes the sailors' expertise sink with them. The only help left is the cry of verse 28.

Finally the psalm ends with the verb bin in verse 43, 'consider,' which is the verb of careful discernment, the root of the word for understanding. The wise person is one who sees the connections between events and the LORD's chesed. That word, loving devotion, is the psalm's last, appearing at verse 1, in the refrains of verses 8, 15, 21 and 31, and again at verse 43, so that the song is wrapped in it.

typology.type: The sea stilled by a word, verses 25 to 30
typology.fulfillment: The LORD raises and quiets the storm. In Mark 4:39 Jesus rebukes the wind and says to the sea, 'Silence! Be still!' and the disciples ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:41. The question has an answer the psalm and Psalm 89:9 had already given: this is the One who rules the raging sea. Matthew 14:32 repeats the pattern when Jesus walks on the water and calms the wind. The escalation is that the disciples are in the boat with the LORD Himself, asleep in the stern. The type falls short in that the psalm's sailors cry to a God they cannot see; the disciples cry to a man in the boat who is God.

typology.type: Prisoners freed from darkness and bars of iron, verses 10 to 16
typology.fulfillment: Christ announces release to the captives, Luke 4:18, quoting Isaiah 61:1, and brings people out of 'darkness and the shadow of death.' Zechariah's song uses the same words of light for those who sit in that darkness, Luke 1:79. The apostles are literally freed from prison by angels, Acts 12:7 to 10, and Paul describes the deeper rescue as being delivered from the domain of darkness into the kingdom of the Son, Colossians 1:13. The type falls short because bronze gates open for a few, while the gospel breaks the power of sin and death for all who believe.

typology.type: Healing by a sent word, verses 17 to 20
typology.fulfillment: God 'sent forth His word and healed them.' The centurion understood this when he told Jesus, 'just say the word, and my servant will be healed,' Matthew 8:8, and the Gospels record many healings by a word. John goes further and names the Word as a person who was with God and was God, John 1:1 and 14. The escalation is that the word the psalm speaks of as an instrument becomes a person who enters the world. The type falls short because every healing in the Gospels was temporary, while the Word Himself will raise the body at the last day.

typology.type: Wanderers brought to a city and filled, verses 4 to 9
typology.fulfillment: The hungry who find no path to a city are led by a straight way to one where they can live. The writer to the Hebrews says the patriarchs sought a better country and that God has prepared a city for them, Hebrews 11:16. Jesus says He fills the hungry, John 6:35, and Revelation promises that those who come out of the great tribulation will never hunger or thirst again, Revelation 7:16. The type falls short because the city of the psalm is a settlement on earth, while the city of the gospel is the new Jerusalem, Revelation 21:2.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the identity of its rescuer. Everything done in the four scenes is done by the LORD alone: He leads, He breaks, He sends His word, He stills the sea. Then the Gospels show Jesus doing these very things. He guides lost people, Luke 15:4. He breaks chains, Mark 5:3 to 15. He heals with a word, Matthew 8:16. He commands the sea, Mark 4:39. The disciples, who sang this psalm, ask, 'Who is this?' Mark 4:41. The psalm has already told them: it is the LORD who 'calmed the storm to a whisper,' and so the question leads to the confession of the Son of God. Matthew's version ends with the disciples worshipping Him, Matthew 14:33.

It leads to Christ by the shape of the refrain. 'Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble' is the cry of the desperate, and Jesus welcomes the cries of the desperate: the blind man at Jericho, Luke 18:38 and 39, the father who says, 'I believe; help my unbelief,' Mark 9:24, the thief on the cross, Luke 23:42. In each case the cry is answered. The psalm gives the pattern, and the Gospels give the person who stands in it.

It leads to Christ in the matter of redemption. The 'redeemed of the LORD' are those bought back from the hand of the enemy, verse 2. The New Testament says that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, Galatians 3:13, and that we have redemption through His blood, Ephesians 1:7. The family image behind the word, a near kinsman who pays the price, is fulfilled when the Son becomes flesh and blood to rescue His brothers, Hebrews 2:14 to 17.

The gathering of verse 3 points to Christ as well. The text speaks of people from east and west, north and south. Jesus says that many will come from east and west to sit at the feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Matthew 8:11, and in Revelation that gathering is a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language, Revelation 7:9. The scattered children of God are gathered into one by His death, John 11:52.

A caution is needed. The psalm does not predict a coming Messiah. Its fourfold rescue belongs to the LORD, and the link to Jesus is that He is the LORD present among His people. Treating the sailors as a code for the church or the storm as a code for judgment would go further than the text. The most that can be said is that Mark deliberately tells the story of the storm in the words of the psalm, and invites the reader to see who is in the boat.
study.god:
This psalm shows a God who hears. The refrain 'Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble' appears four times, and four times is followed by deliverance. The cry does not have to be well formed, and the cause of the trouble does not have to be clean. The prisoners had rebelled, the fools had brought their illness on themselves, the lost travelers may have strayed, and the sailors may have been innocent. The God of the psalm answers them all in the same way, which tells us that His readiness to rescue depends on His character and not on the merit of the one in need.

He is also the God of nature and history. The tempest that terrifies the sailors is something He 'spoke' into being, verse 25, and the calm that follows is also His word. He is not a God who is merely present beside the storm; He commands it. He also turns rivers to desert and desert to springs, verses 33 to 35, and He lifts the needy and humbles the mighty, verses 39 to 41. This sovereignty cuts two ways. It is the ground of hope for those who are low, and a warning to those who trust in position. The psalm adds that the 'nobles' who are made to wander in a trackless waste are not able to save themselves any more than the sailors could, verse 40.

His discipline is part of His goodness. The phrase 'He humbled their hearts with hard labor,' verse 12, is not a statement of cruelty. The purpose of the hardship was to bring the rebellious to the point of crying out. The psalm can then say of the same God that He 'broke away their chains.' Judgment and mercy come from the same hand and serve the same end. This fits Hebrews 12:10, where discipline is given for our good so that we may share in His holiness.

He is the God of chesed. The word opens the psalm, closes it, and sits in each thanks refrain. It means loyal covenant love, the kind that holds on when the partner has failed. The psalm does not pretend that Israel was always faithful. It is the other way around: because the LORD's love endures, the lost can be found, the bound can be freed and the dying can be healed.

His rescue is intended to produce praise. He is not merely a helper who disappears after the job is done. The psalm asks that the rescued should 'declare His works with rejoicing' and exalt Him 'in the assembly of the people,' so that others learn who He is. For worship, this means that thanksgiving is part of the rescue and not an add-on. A person who tells the story of what God has done fulfills the purpose for which the help was given.

And He is the God who invites reflection. 'Let him who is wise pay heed.' He does not demand blind trust; He puts His works before His people and expects them to think about them. The best response to the four scenes is neither a quick emotion nor an abstract theory, but a settled understanding of who He is, built up over a lifetime of noticing His loving devotion.

crossReferences.note: The close of Psalm 106 records that God heard Israel's cry and remembered His covenant, then prays 'gather us from the nations.' Psalm 107:1 to 3 answers that prayer, so the two psalms form one unit across the seam between Books IV and V.

Isaiah describes a highway on which the redeemed of the LORD walk and return to Zion with singing. It shares the psalm's word for the redeemed and its picture of a rescued people coming home, and shows how the prophets and the psalmist drew from the same hope.

The LORD promises to bring His offspring from the east and west, and to say to the north and south, 'Do not hold them back.' The four directions match verse 3, and the promise to gather the people whom He created for His glory supplies the reason behind the redeemed's thanks.

The LORD tells Cyrus that He will break down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron. The same words appear in verse 16, and the parallel shows that the psalm's liberation is rooted in the prophetic promise of release from Babylon.

A storm sent by the LORD terrifies seasoned sailors, who cry to their gods, and then calms when the cause is dealt with. It echoes verses 25 to 30, including the point that the LORD raises the storm, and shows the sailors' fear turning into awe of Him.

Job says God pours out contempt on nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland. Verse 40 repeats nearly the same words, which shows the psalmist drawing on the older wisdom tradition to make the point that rank offers no protection from God.

The centurion asks Jesus to 'just say the word,' and the servant is healed. The scene shows a Gentile recognising what verse 20 had said of the LORD, that His word heals, and it points to the identity of the One speaking.

Jesus is asleep in the boat when a squall comes, and He stills the wind and sea with a word. The disciples ask who He is. The scene is the most direct echo of verses 23 to 30, and it asks the reader to see the LORD of the psalm in the man in the boat.

Mary's song says God has filled the hungry with good things. It echoes verse 9, and shows the Gospel writers treating the psalm's picture of God satisfying the thirsty and hungry as a promise reaching its fulfilment in the coming of the Messiah.

Jesus is asked whether suffering was caused by sin, and He denies the simple link. It balances verses 11 and 17, which tie some suffering to rebellion, by reminding the reader that not every affliction can be traced to a cause.

Hosea closes his book with the call to the wise to understand these things. It matches verse 43, and shows that the prophets and psalmists shared a conviction that the right response to God's dealings is reflection on His ways.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 107 stands where the Bible's story has just reached a low point and begun to turn. Book IV closed with a scattered people pleading to be gathered, and here the gathered ones speak. The pattern of the psalm is the pattern of the whole Bible in small. Humanity wanders away from the garden into a desert, Genesis 3:24, falls into captivity to sin and death, grows sick at heart, and is tossed on a sea it cannot master. The Bible's answer, repeated over and over, is that God hears the cry and acts. The Exodus is the great prototype, a people in bondage whose groaning rose to God, Exodus 2:23 to 25, and who were led through the sea and through the wilderness to a land. The psalm is a distilled retelling of that story with the cast widened to include any person in any trouble.

What the psalm sets up is the question of who this Rescuer is and how a rescue could ever be final. The four rescues in the psalm are real but temporary. The prisoner is freed and later dies. The sick are healed and later die. The sailor reaches harbour and sails again. The psalm itself hints at this with its last section on reversals, in which the same God who raises can also lower. The prophets answer by promising a final redemption in which the deeper problems of sin and death are addressed, Isaiah 25:8 and 53:5 to 6.

In Christ, the psalm's pattern becomes personal and permanent. The Rescuer steps into the boat, takes on flesh and blood, and breaks the bonds of death, Hebrews 2:14 and 15. The word that heals becomes a Word made flesh, John 1:14. The redeemed whom He gathers come from east and west, Matthew 8:11, and the thanks they give is the testimony of the church, which declares what He has done, 1 Peter 2:9. Believers still cry out in their troubles, and they still find that He hears, but they now know the final shape of the answer, Romans 8:35 to 39.

The new creation completes the psalm in a way its first singers could only dimly see. In Revelation the sea is no more, Revelation 21:1, so the sailors' terror has no place. There is no more hunger or thirst, Revelation 7:16, and no more darkness, Revelation 22:5. The prisoners' chains are gone, for the first things have passed away and death is no more, Revelation 21:4. The redeemed of the LORD stand before the throne and say so, and their testimony is the song of Moses and of the Lamb, Revelation 15:3, in which the wisdom of the final verse is fulfilled: they have considered the loving devotion of the LORD and have come to see it fully.

sermon.title: Considering the Great Love of God
sermon.why: Preached by Keller at Redeemer Presbyterian Church from Psalm 107:31-43 as part of the series Four Ways to Live, Four Ways to Love, this sermon works directly from this psalm's closing call to consider the loving devotion of the LORD, drawing out how God's steadfast love, seen across the psalm's four rescue scenes, reorders how His people live and love in response.

quiz.q: Who is invited to speak in verse 2?

options.text: The redeemed of the LORD, those He has redeemed from the hand of the enemy.
options.note: The psalm's opening call is for those who have actually experienced God's rescue to publicly say so.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The call is to the redeemed generally, not restricted to a priestly office.

options.text: The kings of the surrounding nations.
options.note: The psalm addresses Israel's own redeemed people, not foreign kings.

options.text: Only those who have never experienced trouble.
options.note: The whole psalm is about those who were in genuine distress before being redeemed, not those untouched by trouble.

quiz.q: What is the repeated four-part pattern in each of the psalm's rescue scenes?

options.text: Crisis, a cry to the LORD, rescue, and a call to give thanks.
options.note: This exact cycle repeats for wanderers, prisoners, the sick, and sailors alike, verses 4-9, 10-16, 17-22, and 23-32.

options.text: Crisis, self-rescue, pride, and silence.
options.note: The pattern is the opposite: each group is helpless and cries out to the LORD, who alone rescues them.

options.text: Warning, punishment, exile, and return.
options.note: This describes the broader history behind Book V, but the specific repeated pattern within each of the four scenes is crisis, cry, rescue, and thanks.

options.text: Prayer, fasting, sacrifice, and silence.
options.note: The specific repeated elements named in the text are crying out and giving thanks, not a fasting and sacrifice ritual in each scene.

quiz.q: What does God do for the sailors caught in the storm, verse 29?

options.text: He calms the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea are hushed.
options.note: This is the exact scene Jesus reenacts in Mark 4:35-41, commanding the wind and waves with the same authority.

options.text: He sends another ship to rescue them by force.
options.note: The text says God Himself calms the storm directly, not through a rescue vessel.

options.text: He teaches them better navigation skills.
options.note: Verse 27 says their own skill was useless; the rescue comes from God stilling the storm, not from improved sailing technique.

options.text: He allows the ship to sink but saves the sailors individually.
options.note: The text says the storm itself is calmed and the ship reaches its desired harbor, verse 30, not that the ship sinks.

quiz.q: According to verse 43, what should the wise person do?

options.text: Pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD.
options.note: The psalm closes by turning its four rescue stories into an invitation to reflect on and learn from God's steadfast love.

options.text: Avoid all risk and stay away from the sea, the desert, and prison.
options.note: The point is not risk-avoidance but recognizing and considering God's loving devotion in the midst of real distress.

options.text: Trust only in personal skill and preparation.
options.note: The psalm repeatedly shows human skill failing, verse 27, while God's rescue is what actually saves.

options.text: Forget the past and focus only on future plans.
options.note: The wise response named is to consider, remember, and reflect on God's loving devotion, not to forget the past.

quiz.q: How does this psalm connect most directly to the Gospels?

options.text: Jesus calms a storm with the same divine authority this psalm attributes to God alone, verse 29 and Mark 4:35-41.
options.note: The disciples' question, who is this that even wind and sea obey Him, is directly answered by this psalm's own claim about who commands the sea.

options.text: It has no connection to the Gospels.
options.note: Mark 4:35-41 deliberately echoes this exact scene and language.

options.text: It predicts the specific date of a future storm.
options.note: The psalm describes a pattern of rescue, not a prediction of a specific date or storm.

options.text: It is fulfilled only through advances in modern navigation.
options.note: The psalm's deepest fulfillment is Christ's authority over creation itself, not human technological progress.

questions: The psalm calls the redeemed to say so, verse 2, to publicly testify to God's rescue. What story of God's deliverance in your own life have you kept too private that needs to be spoken aloud?

Each of the four scenes follows the same pattern, crisis, cry, rescue, thanks. Which of the four pictures, wandering, imprisonment, sickness, or the storm, most describes where you are right now, and have you cried out to the LORD in it?
Verse 27 says the sailors' own skill was useless in the storm. Where are you relying on your own competence in a situation that actually calls for crying out to God instead?

Jesus calms the very kind of storm this psalm describes, revealing His divine authority, Mark 4:35-41. How does knowing that Christ Himself holds this same power over your storms change your prayers this week?

The psalm ends by calling the wise to consider the loving devotion of the LORD, verse 43. What would it look like this week to deliberately set aside time to consider, not just experience, God's steadfast love?

This psalm opens Book V by picking up the very refrain that closed Book IV. How does seeing your own life as one more chapter in this same, ongoing story of God's redeeming love shape your sense of belonging to His people?

translationNotes.note: From north and south renders a Hebrew phrase literally meaning from the north and the sea, an idiom for the western direction; either way the verse pictures the redeemed gathered from every point of the compass.
All their skill was useless can also be rendered all their wisdom was swallowed up or they were at their wits' end, each capturing the sailors' total helplessness apart from God's rescue.
The waves of the sea follows the Dead Sea Scrolls; the Masoretic Text reads their waves, a minor variant that does not affect the meaning, God silencing the storm completely.
